title: rewardBudget reset to balance + mintDebt on every recompute double-counts already-committed accrual, over-committing emissions and DoSing late claimers
description: `_recomputeSchedule` unconditionally sets `rewardBudget = V = balanceOf(this) + mintDebt` (lines 365-376) without subtracting the portion that the immediately-preceding `_updatePool` call has just committed to `accRewardPerShare`. `_updatePool` advances `accRewardPerShare` by `X = elapsed * rewardRate`, decrements `rewardBudget` by X, but DOES NOT reduce `balance` (the rewards remain in the contract until the staker actually claims). The very next line of `_recomputeSchedule` reads V from balance (which still contains X) and reassigns `rewardBudget = V`, restoring the pre-accrual value. The new `windowEnd = now + V/R` then promises a fresh full runway on top of debt that is already promised. Cumulative emissions over the new window exceed the on-chain balance. The behaviour repeats at every recompute-after-accrual; under the spec's pull-on-interaction model every stake/unstake/claim/topUp/setTargetAPY/pullAndRefresh fires a recompute, so the shortfall accumulates rapidly under normal traffic.
impact: Cumulative emissions exceed on-chain balance. First claimers are paid in full; later claimers hit `_safePay` and revert with `"NFTStaker: insufficient reward balance"`. Earned rewards become stranded until owner top-up. Principal is recoverable via `emergencyWithdraw` but rewards forfeited on that path. Documented invariant `balance == rewardBudget + totalDebt` (totalDebt NatSpec, L488-491) is broken at every recompute by exactly X.
attack_path:
1. Alice stakes at t=0; rewardBudget set to balance V0.
2. Time passes. Alice accrues pending; balance and rewardBudget both stale at V0 (no interaction has fired _updatePool).
3. Bob stakes: _syncBudget runs _updatePool which commits X = elapsed*rewardRate to accRewardPerShare and decrements rewardBudget to V0 - X. Then _recomputeSchedule overwrites rewardBudget = balance + mintDebt = V0 + 0 (balance unchanged because no claim has fired). windowEnd extended.
4. Over the next runway both stakers accrue against an inflated budget. Alice claims first and is paid in full; Bob's claim then reverts because balance < pending.
5. PoC in reports/phoenix-nft-staking-05/audit/pocs demonstrates ~246.58 ether shortfall (~8% of seed) after a single 30-day gap on a 3000-ether seeded budget at 30% APY.
recommendation: In `_recomputeSchedule` subtract committed-but-unclaimed accrual from V before assigning to rewardBudget. The simplest correct expression is `committed = totalDebt(); budget = V > committed ? V - committed : 0;` then `rewardBudget = budget; runway = budget / newRate;`. Equivalent fix: track `rewardBudget` as a monotonic counter and have `_recomputeSchedule` only fold inflow delta into it rather than re-reading balance.

title: emergencyWithdraw decrements totalStaked without calling _updatePool, retroactively repricing pre-withdrawal accrual at the post-withdrawal denominator
description: `emergencyWithdraw` mutates `totalStaked` (line 458) and the user's amount/rewardDebt without first calling `_updatePool` to settle accrual since `lastRewardTime`. As a result, when the next `_updatePool` fires (on a later stake/unstake/claim/admin action), it computes accrual over an elapsed window that spans BOTH the pre- and post-emergency-withdraw periods but divides by the CURRENT (smaller) `totalStaked`. The forfeiting staker's intended-to-be-forfeit accrual is therefore retroactively redistributed pro-rata to the surviving stakers rather than retained by the protocol. `_updatePool` itself is internal and side-effect-free with respect to dispatcher liveness, so calling it from emergencyWithdraw does not violate the documented "escape-hatch" property that emergencyWithdraw must work even when dispatcher / NFT minter / recompute path is broken.
impact: Protocol over-emits rewards relative to the advertised rewardRate * elapsed. Surviving stakers receive a windfall they did not earn under the intended schedule; in concert with ECON-001 this directly amplifies the late-claimer DoS by enlarging the over-committed pool faster than balance can grow. Forfeited rewards do not stay with the protocol as the spec narrative implies — they are redistributed.
attack_path:
1. Alice and Bob each stake 10 at t=0; totalStaked=20.
2. Bob calls emergencyWithdraw at t=100. totalStaked drops to 10. lastRewardTime is still t=0; accRewardPerShare is unchanged (no _updatePool fired).
3. At t=200 Alice calls claim. _updatePool computes elapsed=200, reward = 200*R. accRewardPerShare advanced by 200*R*1e18/10. Alice's pending = 10 * (200*R*1e18/10)/1e18 = 200R.
4. Fair allocation: Alice should earn 50R for [0,100] (pool of 20) plus 100R for [100,200] (pool of 10) = 150R, with 50R retained by the protocol. Actual: Alice receives 200R; 50R is silently redirected from Bob's forfeit to Alice.
5. A coordinated griefer can accelerate the asymmetry by emergency-withdrawing strategically right before a whale unstake, shifting forfeited rewards to whichever surviving staker claims first.
recommendation: Add `_updatePool();` as the first statement in `emergencyWithdraw`, before the require/balance reads. _updatePool short-circuits when totalStaked==0 and only touches storage when totalStaked>0 (no external call), preserving the dispatcher-independence guarantee. Equivalent: settle accrual at the pre-emergency totalStaked denominator before mutating it.

title: rewardRate sized against aggregate minted NFT notional but distributed across totalStaked allows a lone staker to capture the full T-derived stream at unbounded effective APY
description: `_recomputeSchedule` computes `T` as the closed-form aggregate notional of ALL minted NFTs in the dispatcher (`N = nftMinter.totalSupply(stakedId)`), then sets `rewardRate = T * targetAPY / SECONDS_PER_YEAR`. `_updatePool` distributes that aggregate-sized rate across `totalStaked` only. With growthBasisPoints==0 the per-NFT effective APY is `targetAPY * N / totalStaked`, unbounded above when totalStaked is small. Spec frames the math as an APY-as-floor at full participation, which is honoured, but the symmetric ceiling is unbounded and undocumented.
impact: (a) Reward budget depletes up to N times faster than the advertised targetAPY suggests whenever participation is low. (b) Variable-runway design's central narrative ("runway is V/R") silently breaks: actual burn rate is up to N/totalStaked larger than R. (c) Early/opportunistic stakers capture disproportionate shares of emissions at the expense of late stakers and passive holders. (d) Operator cannot accurately forecast V/R as user-visible runway; either over-funds (capital inefficient) or under-funds (premature depletion). PoC in reports/phoenix-nft-staking-05/audit/pocs/poc-M-03 demonstrates 100x effective APY (5000% on a 50% target with N=100, totalStaked=1).
attack_path:
1. Operator launches with N=100 minted NFTs at price=100 ether, growthBP=0, targetAPY=50% (MAX). T=10_000 ether, R=5_000 ether/year. Seed budget V=10_000 ether intended for ~2 years runway.
2. A sophisticated user mints/acquires a single NFT and stakes it before any other holder. totalStaked=1. Effective APY on that 1 NFT = 50% * 100/1 = 5000%.
3. Per-staker pendingReward grows at the full T-sized rate; budget drains at 100x the advertised pace.
4. Late stakers (and passive holders who never stake) find the runway exhausted long before the operator-intended window.
recommendation: Replace the T-based rate with a count-based rate anchored to the current mint price: `F = totalStaked * currentMintPrice * targetAPY / 1e18; rewardRate = F / SECONDS_PER_YEAR`. The latest minter (who paid currentMintPrice) earns exactly targetAPY; earlier minters who paid less earn proportionally more (a multiple of the floor), preserving the spec's APY-floor framing. This eliminates the low-participation multiplier without requiring per-token notional bookkeeping; the only inputs are totalStaked and currentMintPrice, both already available. Document the resulting APY as a floor in the UI and in the spec.

title: _recomputeSchedule reads balanceOf(this) directly, allowing donation griefing to extend runway and amplify the budget-reinflation bug
description: `_recomputeSchedule` reads `rewardToken.balanceOf(address(this))` directly into V, so anyone can transfer phUSD into the staker and have the donation absorbed into rewardBudget on the next recompute. No event is emitted for the donation itself. Combined with ECON-001, a small donation triggered just before a recompute adds donor capital to the inflated budget, further widening the over-commitment window.
impact: Schedule predictability impacted. A donor can anonymously seed the contract before a config change to swing the schedule outside the operator's intent. No direct fund loss because emissions are split across stakers proportionally.
attack_path:
1. Owner intends to call setTargetAPY in a crowded mempool to lower the rate.
2. Attacker front-runs with a 1-wei phUSD transfer to the staker.
3. Subsequent setTargetAPY recomputes V from the new balance and re-opens runway against the donor-inflated budget. With ECON-001 active, prior committed debt is once again re-exposed to fresh emissions.
recommendation: Track rewardBudget as an internal monotonic counter mutated only by topUp and the pull-delta inside _syncBudget. Drop the direct balanceOf read inside _recomputeSchedule. This naturally fixes ECON-001 by removing the re-inflation surface and removes the donation grief vector at the same time.

title: setTargetAPY settles prior accrual using current totalStaked, mispricing the pre-setter window if an emergencyWithdraw shrunk totalStaked since lastRewardTime
description: `setTargetAPY` calls `_updatePool()` to settle old-rate accrual before mutating targetAPY. _updatePool correctly uses the OLD rewardRate (because _recomputeSchedule has not yet fired) but divides by the CURRENT totalStaked. If totalStaked has shrunk since lastRewardTime via emergencyWithdraw (ECON-002), the pre-settlement window is repriced at the smaller denominator — stacking another retroactive shift on top of the emergency redistribution.
impact: Strict child of ECON-002: makes the over-emission strictly worse whenever an APY change coincides with a recent emergencyWithdraw. Not an independent attack path.
attack_path:
1. Alice and Bob stake at t=0 (totalStaked=20).
2. Bob emergencyWithdraws at t=100; totalStaked drops to 10; lastRewardTime still t=0.
3. Owner calls setTargetAPY at t=150. _updatePool accrues with elapsed=150 against totalStaked=10, over-crediting Alice for the [0,100] window twice (the 20-staker and 10-staker share).
recommendation: Fix ECON-002 (call _updatePool inside emergencyWithdraw). With that fix, totalStaked is always settled before being mutated and this finding goes away.

title: pendingReward view diverges from what claim() actually pays under both ECON-001 (insolvency) and dispatcher-side mintDebt growth
description: `pendingReward` simulates the next `_updatePool` step but DOES NOT (a) cap the result at the on-chain reward token balance, nor (b) simulate the next `_syncBudget` (no notional `pull()` on the dispatcher hook, no _recomputeSchedule). Two distinct divergence vectors result: (i) under ECON-001, pendingReward reports a value that claim() will revert on (`_safePay` shortfall); (ii) under healthy operation, pendingReward returns the value computed against the LAST-recomputed rewardRate/rewardBudget rather than the value claim() will produce after refreshing the schedule against current mintDebt and balance. Front-ends, indexers and auto-compounders that consume pendingReward as authoritative claimable receive misleading numbers in both regimes.
impact: UX and integrator impact only. Combined with ECON-001, surfaces as front-ends enabling a Claim button that reverts on submission, eroding user trust. No direct asset loss.
attack_path:
1. ECON-001 scenario plays out, or dispatcher mintDebt grows since the last recompute.
2. Alice queries pendingReward and sees value X.
3. Alice's front-end shows X as claimable. Alice calls claim and either reverts (case i) or receives a different-than-X amount (case ii).
recommendation: Either cap the view at `min(balanceOf(this), pending)` and document that as 'claimable now', or rename / document the function as 'earned but not necessarily payable' and add a sibling simulating _syncBudget. The deeper correctness fix is ECON-001.

title: dispatcher hook mintDebt() is unconditionally trusted as available value in V; a hostile or buggy hook can over-commit emissions and DoS claims
description: `_recomputeSchedule` adds `dispatcherHook.mintDebt()` directly to V, which becomes both rewardBudget and the basis for windowEnd. _syncBudget measures actual inflow via balance delta around `pull()`, but _recomputeSchedule trusts mintDebt for accounting. A dispatcher hook that reports mintDebt larger than it will actually mint on pull() inflates the scheduled runway and lets the contract commit to emissions it cannot pay. setDispatcherHook has no `totalStaked == 0` guard (hook rotation is by design a live operation), so this is exercisable without unwinding the pool. Routes through owner action and is therefore a centralization risk rather than an external-attacker path.
impact: Stakers' accrued rewards become unpayable (frozen behind _safePay revert) when the owner installs a hostile or buggy dispatcher hook. Recovery requires owner topUp or users taking emergencyWithdraw (forfeiting rewards). Principal is always recoverable.
attack_path:
1. Owner (or compromised owner key) installs a dispatcher hook whose mintDebt() returns a huge number but whose pull() mints little.
2. Any user calls stake/unstake/claim. _syncBudget invokes pull() (balance delta ~0); _recomputeSchedule reads V = balance + hugeMintDebt and extends windowEnd accordingly.
3. Stakers accrue against the inflated rate. Eventually balance < pending for every staker and all claims revert.
4. Recovery: owner topUp, or users take emergencyWithdraw and forfeit rewards.
recommendation: Drop mintDebt() from the V computation inside _recomputeSchedule (only count actual balance), accepting a small lag between pulls. Alternatively cap V at `balance + (mintDebt - inflow_just_pulled)` and validate that pull() actually drained most of mintDebt. The current design trusts an external hook for emission scheduling, which is the centralization surface.

title: setDispatcherHook rotation orphans the OLD hook's outstanding mintDebt and leaves rewardBudget stale until corrective action
description: setDispatcherHook is the only owner-only setter in this contract that does NOT call _syncBudget / _recomputeSchedule and is NOT gated on `totalStaked == 0`. After rotation, pull() targets the new hook only — any outstanding mintDebt at the old hook becomes unreachable on-chain. The previously computed rewardBudget (which included old_hook.mintDebt()) is now stale and inflated relative to actual realisable value. The next _syncBudget runs _updatePool against the stale budget at the stale rewardRate, advancing accRewardPerShare against value the contract cannot redeem.
impact: Reward flow can be bricked between rotation and corrective action. Principal is recoverable via emergencyWithdraw; rewards forfeit on that path. Recovery requires owner topUp covering the gap or installing a hook with sufficient debt to replace the lost mintDebt.
attack_path:
1. Owner routinely rotates dispatcherHook while the OLD hook still has outstanding mintDebt.
2. Outstanding mintDebt becomes unreachable: pull() now targets the NEW hook.
3. rewardBudget remains inflated from the prior _recomputeSchedule that included the old hook's mintDebt.
4. Subsequent user interactions advance accRewardPerShare against the stale budget; _safePay starts reverting.
5. Recovery: owner topUp or install a replacement hook with sufficient debt to cover the gap.
recommendation: Either (a) gate setDispatcherHook on `totalStaked == 0` to match sibling setters, or (b) call `_syncBudget()` inside setDispatcherHook BEFORE writing the new hook reference (so the old hook's mintDebt is realised first), then call `_recomputeSchedule()` after to re-anchor the schedule on the new hook. Sibling setters (setDispatcherIndex / setNFTMinter) follow option (b)'s shape; this setter is the inconsistent outlier.

title: Owner can zero out emissions mid-stake via setTargetAPY(0) or setDispatcherHook(address(0)); no timelock or notice on a user-facing APY commitment
description: setTargetAPY(0) is explicitly permitted and immediately drops rewardRate to 0 (per CLAUDE.md item 7: 'A == 0 is a supported pause emissions via APY mode'). Old accrual is settled at the old rate, but advertised future runway evaporates with no notice or on-chain timelock. setDispatcherHook(address(0)) similarly removes the pull() path and lets the budget drain without further inflows. The targetAPY surface is the user-facing commitment of the pool; the absence of any notice window or monotonicity rule means the operator can unilaterally cancel that commitment.
impact: Stakers committed NFTs based on a published targetAPY for a published runway. Owner can collapse that runway to zero with no on-chain compensation. Pure centralization. No external-attacker path.
attack_path:
1. Users commit NFTs based on a visible targetAPY of 30% with a multi-year runway.
2. Owner calls setTargetAPY(0) immediately after a large stake. Runway collapses to zero.
3. Users unstake and receive only the accrual up to the setter timestamp; the advertised future APY is lost.
recommendation: If the targetAPY is intended as a commitment, add a minimum-notice queue (e.g. APY decreases delayed by 7 days) and/or a monotonicity rule (rate can only fall by at most X% per tx). Alternatively, document explicitly that the APY is mutable at any moment without notice and surface that in the UI.

title: setStakedId mutates the active token ID without recomputing the emission schedule; runway/rewardRate views remain stale until next interaction
description: setStakedId is gated on `totalStaked == 0` and writes the new stakedId, but unlike its sister setters setDispatcherIndex (line 218) and setNFTMinter (line 229) it does NOT call `_recomputeSchedule()` after mutation. Because rewardRate is derived from `nftMinter.totalSupply(stakedId)`, changing stakedId changes T. Until the next user-triggered _syncBudget runs, rewardRate / rewardBudget / windowEnd retain the values computed against the previous token ID. External views (currentRewardRate, runwaySeconds, pendingReward, totalDebt) and off-chain integrations report stale values.
impact: No principal or reward leak (totalStaked==0 short-circuits _updatePool). Inconsistent state surface between sibling admin setters, and front-ends driven by ScheduleRecomputed events report a stale schedule between setStakedId and the first subsequent recompute trigger.
attack_path:
1. Owner calls setStakedId(newId) when totalStaked==0.
2. nftMinter.totalSupply(newId) differs from totalSupply(oldId), but rewardRate / windowEnd remain the values computed against oldId.
3. Off-chain consumers query currentRewardRate / runwaySeconds and see values inconsistent with on-chain config until a stake / unstake / claim / pullAndRefresh fires.
recommendation: Append `_recomputeSchedule();` to setStakedId, mirroring setDispatcherIndex and setNFTMinter. Alternatively, document explicitly why this setter intentionally leaves the schedule stale.

title: setPauser accepts address(0), silently disabling the pause/unpause capability
description: setPauser performs no input validation. Because the onlyPauser modifier compares `msg.sender == pauser`, setting pauser = address(0) effectively disables pause()/unpause() (no msg.sender can equal address(0) under normal EVM invariants). The global Pauser registration flow expects this contract to be pause-able on demand; an accidental zero assignment silently breaks that emergency invariant. Recoverable by a subsequent owner call but no on-chain guard against the misconfiguration window.
impact: Operational risk: a separately-discovered exploitable vulnerability cannot be mitigated via pause() during the window in which pauser is mis-set. No external-attacker path.
attack_path:
1. Owner script deploys with an empty env variable resolving to address(0) for the pauser.
2. Or owner fat-fingers and calls setPauser(address(0)).
3. Pause/unpause is now non-functional; no on-chain alarm.
4. A separately-discovered vulnerability that requires an emergency pause cannot be mitigated until owner re-sets pauser.
recommendation: Add `require(newPauser != address(0), "NFTStaker: zero pauser");` to setPauser, OR explicitly document that address(0) is a deliberate 'pause disabled' state (and add a separate capability-disable function so the intent is explicit).

title: Admin setters (setDispatcherHook, setNFTMinter) do not validate that the supplied address conforms to the expected interface
description: setDispatcherHook accepts any address (including non-contracts and unrelated contracts) without validating that the target implements IBalancerPoolerMintDebtHook (mintDebt + pull). setNFTMinter has a zero-address guard but does not validate the INFTSupply interface (configs + totalSupply). A misconfigured address causes _syncBudget / _recomputeSchedule to revert at the external call, blocking stake/unstake/claim. setNFTMinter is gated on totalStaked==0 and the recompute fires inside the setter, so the bad minter is rejected at setter time (the require self-heals). setDispatcherHook has no recompute and no totalStaked gate, so the bad hook persists until the next user action reverts.
impact: setDispatcherHook misconfiguration: pool freezes for stake/unstake/claim until owner re-sets hook; users forced through emergencyWithdraw forfeit rewards. setNFTMinter misconfiguration: setter itself reverts (self-healing). Both are admin-only paths.
attack_path:
1. Owner scripts a deployment with a bad dispatcher hook address (typo, wrong network, unrelated contract).
2. Next stake/unstake/claim reverts at hook.pull() inside _syncBudget.
3. Users either wait for owner to fix or take emergencyWithdraw (forfeiting rewards).
recommendation: Probe interface conformance via low-level staticcall to mintDebt() in setDispatcherHook before persisting; document setNFTMinter's recompute-as-liveness-probe in NatSpec. Optionally also validate `address(newHook).code.length > 0` at setter time.
